questions.questionText: Pretexting relies heavily on human psychological traits like helpfulness, politeness, and respect for authority.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Attackers exploit natural human social tendencies to manipulate targets.

questions.questionText: What is the gold standard rule when handling requests for sensitive corporate information?

options.text: Share the data if the caller sounds friendly.
Verify identity and authorization through official channels before releasing any data.
Always post data on public forums.
Never talk to anyone at work.

questions.explanation: Always verify identity and clearance before transmitting sensitive data.

questions.questionText: What structural control prevents pretexting attempts from compromising internal resources?

options.text: Allowing employees to share passwords freely.
Enforcing strict adherence to official identity verification and ticketing channels.
Removing password locks from work laptops.
Disabling all antivirus software.

questions.explanation: Formal channels and strict verification neutralize pretexting narratives.

questions.questionText: How does pretexting differ from mass phishing?

options.text: Pretexting uses malicious email attachments exclusively.
Pretexting focuses on building a credible narrative and relationship, whereas mass phishing relies on broad, generic lures.
Mass phishing only targets phone landlines.
Pretexting is legally permitted in business.

questions.explanation: Pretexting prioritizes narrative depth and trust over volume.

questions.questionText: What role does flattery play in pretexting interactions?

options.text: It encrypts the user's hard drive.
It lowers the victim's defenses by making them feel valued and eager to assist.
It speeds up internet connection bandwidth.
It triggers automated firewall logging.

questions.explanation: Flattery creates positive rapport, encouraging the target to comply with requests.

questions.questionText: Why do pretexters often try to discourage victims from submitting official IT service tickets?

options.text: IT tickets cost money to create.
Official tickets trigger administrative logs and security reviews that would expose the fake identity.
IT ticketing systems automatically block phone calls.
Scammers prefer using postal mail.

questions.explanation: Formal ticketing creates an audit trail that alerts legitimate security personnel.

questions.questionText: Pretexters never target remote workers who do not have executive titles.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Administrative assistants, support staff, and contractors are frequently targeted for their access to directory data and internal processes.

questions.questionText: You receive a message from a "new vendor" asking for internal directory structures so they can "prepare project integration." You have not received any notification from management about a new vendor. What is the correct protocol?

options.text: Send the directory file immediately.
Do not share internal data; verify the vendor's onboarding status with your internal manager or procurement team.
Ask the vendor to pay you $50.
Send them dummy data containing real employee passwords.

questions.explanation: Unverified third parties must be vetted through management before receiving internal assets.

questions.questionText: Out-of-band verification is ineffective against pretexting.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Independent out-of-band verification effectively exposes pretexts by contacting the real organization or individual.

questions.questionText: A remote worker receives a call from an individual claiming to be a printer technician needing internal Wi-Fi passwords to fix an office printer 500 miles away. Why is this request suspicious?

options.text: Printers do not use electricity.
The scenario lacks logical plausibility, and Wi-Fi credentials should never be shared verbally with external technicians.
Technicians only speak French.
Wi-Fi passwords cannot be typed on laptops.

questions.explanation: Evaluating the logical plausibility of a request helps spot flawed pretexts.
